en: Jātaka:
The Collection of Twenty, Chapter on Mātaṅga
14. The Ayogharajātakasutta:
“The young man who dwells for the first time in the womb for one night;”
He goes forth as soon as he has risen;
having gone his way, he does not turn back.
Not by fighting, nor by force, is he overcome.
Men neither decay nor do they die;
all here are merely afflicted by birth and old age—
this is my conviction, and thus I live according to the Dhamma.
The lords of the realm, by force, conquer a fourfold army of beautiful appearance;
yet they are not able to conquer Death.
This is my conviction: I live according to the Dhamma.
Even those who are surrounded by elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—some of them might even be released.
They do not strive to escape from death;
this is my conviction, and thus I practice the Dhamma.
[I do not flee] with elephants, horses, chariots, or infantry.
The brave shatter and destroy [the ranks of the enemy],
yet they do not dare to shatter Death;
this is my conviction, and thus I practice the Dhamma.
Intoxicated elephants with temples split and flowing,
trample cities and kill people;
yet they are not able to crush Death.
This is my conviction: I live according to the Dhamma.
Though there be heroes who are envious, those who have already struck their hands in action, those who shoot from afar, and those who pierce the mark at once;
Death does not dare to pierce him;
this is my conviction as I practice the Dhamma.
Even the oceans, along with their mountains and forests, dry up.
All this decays over a long interval;
all this breaks down according to the course of time.
This is my conviction: I live in accordance with the Dhamma.
For all men and women alike,
O enjoyer of life, this existence here is fickle and unstable;
it is like a cloth held by a rogue, or like a tree growing on a riverbank.
This is my conviction: I practice the Dhamma.
Like the fruits of a tree, young men and old alike fall when the body breaks up, O youth.
Women, men, and those of middle stature—
this is my thought as I practice the Dhamma.
This age of mine is like the king of stars.
That which has passed away is now gone;
for one who is old, there is no delight, so how could there be happiness?
This is my thought: I practice the Dhamma.
Yakṣas, piśācas, or even pretas,
when enraged, may cause mortals to gasp for breath;
but they cannot make Death itself gasp for breath.
This is my thought: I practice the Dhamma.
Even if yakkhas, pisācas, or even petas are provoked, they bring about a change of heart in me.
They do not bring about Death’s satisfaction;
this is my conviction as I practice the Dhamma.
Toward the offender, the corrupter, and the oppressor—
Kings inflict punishment once they have recognized a fault;
but Death cannot bring down such punishment.
This is my conviction: I live according to the Dhamma.
Those who commit offenses, those who harm others,
and those who act with malice may be brought to judgment by kings;
but they cannot bring death to judgment.
This is my conviction: I practice the Dhamma.
I am neither a kshatriya nor a brahmin, nor am I wealthy, powerful, or majestic.
The King of Death has no regard for me;
this is my conviction as I practice the Dhamma.
Even lions, tigers, and leopards—
They devour one who is writhing after having overcome him;
they do not dare to devour one already devoured by Death—
this is my resolve as I practice the Dhamma.
Just as magicians performing in the midst of a theater deceive the eyes of the people for that time,
they are not able to deceive Death when he seeks to delude them.
This is my conviction: I practice the Dhamma.
Enraged and fierce in their power, venomous serpents bite and even kill human beings.
Even the enraged venomous snakes do not dare to bite that for which I think: "I practice the Dhamma."
Physicians destroy their poison,
but they do not destroy the poison of Death’s bite;
this is my conviction as I practice the Dhamma.
Dhammantari, Vettaraṇī, and Bhoja—
having destroyed the poisons of serpents,
they too, when their time has come, are likewise burned up.
This is my conviction: I practice the Dhamma.
The Vidyādharas, studying their terrible spells, attain invisibility by means of medicinal herbs.
I do not seek an audience with the King of Death;
this is my resolve: I practice the Dhamma.
Indeed, the Dhamma protects the one who walks in the Dhamma.
The Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness;
this is the benefit when the Dhamma is well-practiced:
one who lives according to the Dhamma does not go to a state of misery.
For neither Dhamma nor non-Dhamma both have the same result;
non-Dhamma leads to hell.
“Dhamma leads one to a happy destination.
Thus ends the Fourteenth Jātaka, the Ayogharajātaka.
The Vīsatinipāta is completed.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is:
Mātaṅga, Sambhūta, Sivi, Sirimanta,
Rohaṇa, Haṃsa, Sattigumba, and Bhallātiya.
Somanassa Campeyya Brahma, Pañca,
Paṇḍita, Cirassamvata, and Ayoghara.
